result.summary: Hector, prompted by Apollo and Minerva, challenges the Achaeans to single combat and Ajax, chosen by lot, fights him to a draw until heralds part them at nightfall. After a truce to burn the dead, the Achaeans build a wall and trench, and Neptune complains to Jove.

scenes.title: Gods plan a duel
scenes.summary: Hector and Alexandrus return to battle and kill several Achaeans. Minerva and Apollo meet at the oak and agree to have Hector challenge a Danaan.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans are losing men while the gods decide how the fighting will end.

scenes.title: Hector's challenge
scenes.summary: Helenus urges Hector to challenge the Achaeans. No one answers until Menelaus rises, but Agamemnon restrains him.
scenes.stakes: Menelaus risks death against a stronger man; the Achaeans risk shame.

scenes.title: Nestor recalls Ereuthalion
scenes.summary: Nestor shames the chiefs by recalling how, as a young man, he killed Ereuthalion.
scenes.stakes: Nestor's tale shames the Achaeans' honour.

scenes.title: Lots drawn; Ajax steps forward
scenes.summary: Nine heroes volunteer and the lot falls on Ajax. He arms and faces Hector, and the two trade boasts.
scenes.stakes: Ajax risks his life and the Achaeans' honour.

scenes.title: Ajax and Hector fight
scenes.summary: They hurl spears and stones; Hector is knocked down but raised by Apollo. Heralds part them at night and they exchange gifts.
scenes.stakes: Each risks death; Hector is nearly killed.

scenes.title: Feast and Nestor's plan
scenes.summary: Agamemnon feasts Ajax. Nestor proposes burying the dead and building a wall and trench.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans need protection against the Trojans.

scenes.title: Trojan council
scenes.summary: Antenor urges returning Helen; Alexandrus refuses and Priam sends Idaeus to propose a truce.
scenes.stakes: Troy risks continued war through breaking its oaths.

scenes.title: Truce and burning of the dead
scenes.summary: Idaeus delivers the message; Diomed rejects the offer but Agamemnon grants the truce. Both sides burn their dead.
scenes.stakes: Both armies must honour their dead; Troy's offer is rejected.

scenes.title: The wall and Neptune's complaint
scenes.summary: The Achaeans build the wall and trench. Neptune complains and Jove reassures him. They buy Lemnian wine and feast while Jove thunders.
scenes.stakes: The gods' honour is neglected; the Achaeans face Jove's ill omens.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses both names for Priam's son who took Helen.
Names for the Greeks used interchangeably.

notable_quotes.reason: Hector's hope for lasting fame shows the heroic code.
Neptune's complaint that the wall was built without sacrifices.

analysis.text: Single combat and gift exchange show heroic honour, where foes respect each other, while the gods steer events.
The funeral rites and burial mounds reflect the importance of proper burial in early Greek culture.

legacy.text: The exchange of the sword and girdle between Hector and Ajax became a classic image of chivalrous enemies and has been recalled by later writers.

fun_facts.text: Ajax's sevenfold ox-hide shield became a standard image of the great tower shield in Greek epic.

language_notes.text: This is the book's summary (argument), not part of the poem; it lists events to come, including the Achaeans buying wine.
Mace-man: Areithous was known as a warrior who fought with an iron mace rather than a spear or bow.
Ilius is Troy (Ilium); Pergamus is its citadel, the high fortress of the city.
"Incline the scales" means tip the balance of the war, an image of victory being weighed out.
"You goddesses" refers to Minerva, Juno and others who favour the Greeks and want Troy destroyed, since the Judgment of Paris.
Far-Darter is a title of Apollo, the archer god whose arrows shoot from afar.
"Divined the counsel of the gods" means he perceived their plan, here through prophetic insight; Helenus was a seer.
"The hour of your doom is not yet come" means Hector is not fated to die yet, so the duel is safe for him.
Jove's oak was sacred to him; the gods perch there as vultures, watching the armies like birds over a carcass.
"Dues of fire" means funeral rites: cremation was essential for the dead to find rest in the afterlife.
"Danaans" is another name for the Greeks, like Achaeans; "forsooth" means "truly" and is used here sarcastically.
Menelaus curses them to become "earth and water", meaning to rot away like corpses or lifeless matter.
"I ween" means "I think"; "hurly-burly" means the tumult of battle.
Myrmidons were Peleus' people in Phthia, later led by his son Achilles at Troy.
"Quailing" means shrinking back in fear.
"Would, by father Jove... that I were" is an oath-like wish: "if only I were." Jove is the Greek Zeus.
"Mace" is a heavy club; Areithous fought with an iron one instead of the usual bow or spear.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted.
"Stomach for fighting" means appetite or courage for it; an idiom for willingness.
"The two Ajaxes" are Ajax son of Telamon and the lesser Ajax, son of Oileus. "Brother in arms" means comrade, not blood brother.
"Marked his lot": each hero scratched his own sign on a token so it could be recognised when drawn.
"Owned it" means acknowledged it as theirs; none of the other men claimed the lot.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously; "rulest" is the archaic second-person form of "rule".
Tychius of Hyle is a famous leatherworker, mentioned only for making this shield. Hyle is a town in Boeotia.
"Danaans" is another name for the Greeks, like Argives and Achaeans.
The shield had seven layers of ox-hide covered by an eighth outer layer of bronze, so the spear passed through the bronze and six hides.
Cuirass: a piece of armour protecting the chest and back.
"The behests of night may not be well gainsaid" means night's commands should not be disobeyed; fighting in darkness was unwise.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted or given.
A baldric is a belt worn over the shoulder to carry a sword.
The long loin slices were the choicest cut; giving Ajax the best portion was a formal honour for his valour.
"Wheel our dead together" means haul the bodies in carts drawn by oxen and mules to a common burning place.
"Barrow" is a burial mound of earth heaped over the ashes of the dead.
The "solemn covenants" are the oaths sworn by both sides in Book 3 to abide by the duel of Paris and Menelaus, which the Trojans then broke.
Paris is Alexandrus' other name; the translation uses both for the same man.
"Be instant with them" means urge them earnestly.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war; "servants of Mars" is a stock phrase for warriors.
"If so be that" is archaic for "if it happens that"; Idaeus hopes the Achaeans will find the offer acceptable.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, who carried off Helen and caused the war.
"Let there be no taking" means: accept no offer, neither the treasure nor Helen herself.
Calling Jove as witness makes the truce a sworn covenant, guarded by the chief god and husband of Juno (the Greek Hera).
Oceanus was imagined as a great river encircling the world, from which the sun rose each morning.
A barrow is an earthen burial mound, here raised over the ashes of the dead from the pyre.
Hecatombs were large public sacrifices of cattle, originally a hundred oxen, offered to win the gods' favour.
Neptune refers to the walls of Troy, built for King Laomedon by Neptune and Apollo, who were then cheated of their payment.
Hypsipyle was queen of Lemnos, who bore Jason's son Eueneus; the link recalls the voyage of the Argonauts.
Spilling wine is a libation: the Greeks poured wine to the gods before drinking, and fear makes them do it anxiously.

context_notes.text: Hector, Troy's chief warrior, and his brother Alexandrus (Paris), whose abduction of Helen began the war, return from the city to the battlefield.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) supports the Greeks; Apollo supports Troy.
The oak, probably the sacred oak by the Scaean gates, is a known landmark on the Trojan plain.
Helenus is a son of Priam and brother of Hector, famed as a Trojan prophet.
Ilius is Troy; the Hellespont is the strait now called the Dardanelles, near which the Greek camp lay.
Agamemnon is Menelaus' elder brother and leader of the Achaean army; the war began over Menelaus' wife Helen.
Achilles is the greatest Achaean warrior but is currently sitting out the war in anger at Agamemnon.
Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, is the Achaeans' elder counsellor. He often rebukes or advises the chiefs by recalling his past deeds.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is goddess of war and wisdom, and Apollo a god of prophecy and archery; Nestor invokes them as powers who can restore strength.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war; armour given by a god marks its owner as exceptional.
Diomed (Diomedes) is one of the Greeks' strongest fighters, son of Tydeus.
Salamis is the island home of Ajax and his father Telamon.
Achilles is sulking at the ships after quarrelling with Agamemnon, so the Greeks fight without him.
Apollo favoured the Trojans and often protected Hector.
Heralds were sacred, inviolable officials who carried messages and kept order, and they could halt a combat. Talthybius served the Achaeans and Idaeus the Trojans.
Mars is the god of war (the Greek Ares); Hades is the god and realm of the dead.
Antenor is a respected Trojan elder who elsewhere favours returning Helen; the acropolis is the fortified high part of the city.
Idaeus is Priam's herald, whose person was customarily protected when carrying messages between enemies.
Menelaus, Agamemnon's brother, was Helen's husband. Her abduction is the stated cause of the war.
Proper funeral rites, especially burning the body, were essential in Greek belief for the dead to find rest.
Holding up the sceptre was a gesture of authority when swearing an oath or speaking officially.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea and earthquakes, and he favoured the Achaeans against Troy.
Jove allows Neptune to destroy the wall later; this foreshadows its ruin after the war ends.
Coinage was not used in the poem; goods, metals, hides, cattle and slaves serve as barter.

literary_notes.text: The Trojans' relief at seeing Hector and Alexandrus is likened to tired rowers receiving a wind, showing how exhausted and desperate they were.
Apollo's "proud spirit" taunts Minerva as an eager, partisan goddess, while his courteous tone shows divine politeness masking rivalry.
The plan for a single combat anticipates the duel between Hector and Ajax that gives the book its main action.
The seated armies are likened to the sea darkened by the west wind, evoking their dense, dark, rippling ranks.
Hector's concern for fame and for fair treatment of the dead shows his honor and heroic values.
The Achaeans are ashamed to refuse yet afraid to accept, so their silence exposes the fear they would hide.
The narrator suddenly addresses Menelaus directly, heightening the danger and showing sympathy for him.
Nestor imagines Peleus' grief to shame the Achaeans indirectly, making them feel their cowardice without directly insulting them.
The nickname "the Mace-man" sums up Areithous' unusual fighting style in a single name.
Nestor repeats his wish to be young again, framing the whole story as a contrast between past heroism and present timidity.
Calling them "foremost among the whole host" while accusing them of cowardice is bitterly ironic and sharpens the rebuke.
Valour is described as a garment the Ajaxes wear, picturing courage as protection and as part of their appearance.
The lot Nestor shakes out is the one the army wished for, suggesting divine favour with the choice.
Ajax is compared to Mars, the war god, advancing grimly; the comparison shows his terrifying size and fighting power.
Even Hector's heart pounds, but pride keeps him from retreating, showing both his fear and his honour.
Ajax's shield is likened to a wall, stressing his role as defender, as the epithet "bulwark" also does.
Comparing the fighters to lions and boars conveys their ferocity and equal strength.
Calling the rock a millstone stresses its enormous weight and Ajax's superhuman strength.
The exchanged gifts symbolise mutual respect between enemies; the sword and girdle will later have tragic significance.
"Whose counsel was ever truest" is Nestor's stock description, marking him as the army's wise elder before he speaks.
Paris says heaven has robbed Antenor of reason, yet his own refusal to return Helen is the folly that dooms Troy.
The brief closing statement of obedience shows the Trojan council ending in quiet compliance, after the debate, with the narrator moving on swiftly.
"Of the loud war-cry" is Diomed's fixed Homeric epithet, stressing his battle prowess just before he speaks boldly.
The sun "beating" on the fields and rising from the "slow still currents" gives the dawn a vivid, living quality.
This sentence repeats the previous one almost word for word, showing both sides sharing the same grief and duty.
Titles such as 'lord of the earthquake' and 'lord of lightning' are formulaic epithets that identify each god by his power.
Neptune's complaint is ironic because he himself once built walls for Troy, and the gods are now jealous of mortal building.
Jove's ominous thunder warns of the suffering he will bring to both armies as the war goes on.
